title: Colour Matching Guide
heading: Neutral colours
text: Black, white, grey, navy, beige, tan, and olive are neutrals. Neutrals combine with almost everything, so an outfit built mostly from neutrals is hard to get wrong. A good rule is to keep most of the outfit neutral and add at most one stronger colour or pattern.

title: Colour Matching Guide
heading: Colours that go with navy
text: Navy pairs well with white, grey, beige, tan, olive, and brown. Navy with tan or brown leather is a classic smart casual combination. Navy and black can be worn together when the difference in shade is clear, but the pairing looks best with a light colour, such as a white shirt, between them.

title: Colour Matching Guide
heading: Black and brown
text: Black and brown can be worn together when they are clearly different shades, for example dark jeans with brown boots. For more formal outfits, keep shoes and belt in the same colour family: brown shoes with a brown belt, black shoes with a black belt.

title: Colour Matching Guide
heading: Denim
text: Blue denim acts as a neutral. Dark jeans pair with grey, white, black, olive, navy, and earth tones. Wearing a denim jacket with jeans works best when the two washes differ clearly in shade.

title: Colour Matching Guide
heading: Patterns
text: Wear one pattern at a time, such as a striped scarf or a plaid flannel shirt, and keep the rest plain. Pick the other colours from the colours in the pattern so the outfit looks planned.

title: Dress Code Guide
heading: Casual
text: Casual means everyday clothes chosen for comfort: t-shirts, hoodies, sweaters, jeans, joggers, sneakers, and casual jackets such as a denim or puffer jacket. Casual is right for errands, friends, sport, and relaxed weekends.

title: Dress Code Guide
heading: Smart casual
text: Smart casual sits between casual and business. It means neat, well-fitting clothes without a suit or tie: a collared shirt such as an oxford shirt or a fine knit sweater, chinos or dark well-kept jeans without rips, and leather shoes such as loafers or Chelsea boots. A trench coat or a plain wool coat works as outerwear. Avoid sportswear, hoodies, worn sneakers, and shorts. Smart casual suits dinners at nicer restaurants, dates, and many offices.

title: Dress Code Guide
heading: Business and formal
text: Business dress means a suit with a collared shirt, usually with a tie, and polished leather shoes. Formal or black tie events need a tuxedo or a dark suit. The wardrobe in this project has no suits, so business and formal outfits cannot be built from it.

title: Dress Code Guide
heading: Interviews
text: For a job interview, dress one level more formal than the people who already work there. For a relaxed office that is usually smart casual: a collared shirt, chinos, and leather shoes.

title: Dress Code Guide
heading: Weddings and events
text: A wedding invitation normally states the dress code. If it does not, ask the hosts, because it depends on the venue and the time of day. Avoid wearing white to a wedding as a guest.

title: Fabric Care Guide
heading: Wool sweaters and knitwear
text: Wash wool by hand in cool water (about 30 °C at most) with a wool or mild detergent, or use the wool cycle of the washing machine. Do not wring or twist the garment. Press the water out by rolling it in a towel, then dry it flat on a towel away from radiators and direct sunlight. Hanging wet wool stretches it, and hot water or tumble drying shrinks and felts it. Wool needs washing less often than cotton: airing it out overnight is usually enough between wears.

title: Fabric Care Guide
heading: Pilling on knitwear
text: Pilling is the small fuzzy balls that form on knitted jumpers and sweaters where the fabric rubs, for example under the arms or where a bag strap sits. Remove the pills with a fabric shaver or a sweater comb, working gently on a flat surface. Washing knitwear inside out and on a gentle cycle reduces new pilling. Pilling is normal for wool and does not mean the garment is damaged.

title: Fabric Care Guide
heading: Cotton t-shirts and shirts
text: Cotton t-shirts and shirts can be machine washed at 30–40 °C. Turn printed or dark items inside out to protect the colour. Cotton can shrink a little in a hot tumble dryer, so dry it on low heat or on a hanger. Iron oxford shirts while slightly damp for the best result.

title: Fabric Care Guide
heading: Denim jeans
text: Wash dark denim jeans rarely and inside out in cold water to keep the colour from fading. Skip the tumble dryer and hang them to dry. Spot clean small marks instead of washing the whole pair.

title: Fabric Care Guide
heading: Waterproof rain jackets
text: Clean a waterproof rain jacket with a technical wash, not normal detergent or fabric softener, which clog the membrane. When water stops beading on the surface, re-waterproof the jacket: wash it, then apply a spray-on or wash-in DWR (durable water repellent) treatment, and finish with a short low-heat tumble dry or iron on low heat if the care label allows it, which reactivates the coating.

title: Fabric Care Guide
heading: Hoodies and sweatpants
text: Wash hoodies and jogger sweatpants inside out at 30 °C to limit pilling and fading. Close zips before washing. Air drying keeps the fleece lining soft.

title: Layering and Weather Guide
heading: The three-layer system
text: Dress in layers so you can adjust to the temperature. A base layer next to the skin (t-shirt or thin shirt), a mid layer for warmth (sweater, flannel shirt, or hoodie), and an outer layer against wind and rain (rain jacket, puffer, or coat). Remove or add the mid layer as the day warms or cools.

title: Layering and Weather Guide
heading: Near-freezing and cold days
text: Around 0 °C and below, wear all three layers: a base layer, a warm mid layer such as a wool sweater, and an insulated outer layer such as a puffer jacket. Add a hat such as a wool beanie and a scarf, because a lot of comfort is lost at the head and neck. Choose closed, waterproof boots over sneakers.

title: Layering and Weather Guide
heading: Rainy days
text: For rain, the outer layer and the shoes matter most. Wear a waterproof rain jacket or a trench coat and waterproof boots. Prefer jeans or dark trousers to light-coloured fabrics, which show water marks. Carry an umbrella when the wind is not too strong; in strong wind, a hooded rain jacket is more reliable than an umbrella.

title: Layering and Weather Guide
heading: Windy days
text: Wind makes it feel several degrees colder than the thermometer says. A windproof outer layer such as a rain jacket or puffer blocks the wind, and a scarf and beanie protect the neck and ears.

title: Layering and Weather Guide
heading: Hot and sunny days
text: In heat, choose loose, breathable fabrics such as cotton and light colours that reflect sunlight. Shorts and t-shirts are fine for casual plans. Wear a cap or hat for sun protection and breathable shoes such as canvas sneakers.

title: Layering and Weather Guide
heading: Mild days
text: On mild days of about 14–20 °C, a t-shirt or shirt with a light jacket such as a denim jacket is usually enough. Keep a light layer with you in case the evening cools down.

title: Shoe Care Guide
heading: Suede shoes and boots in wet weather
text: Suede is easily stained by water and salt. Avoid wearing suede shoes such as suede Chelsea boots in rain, slush, or snow. If suede gets wet, blot it with a dry cloth, let it dry naturally at room temperature away from heaters, and brush the nap back up with a suede brush once dry. A suede protector spray reduces water damage but does not make suede waterproof.

title: Shoe Care Guide
heading: Leather shoes and loafers
text: Clean smooth leather shoes with a damp cloth, then apply shoe cream or polish every few weeks to keep the leather supple. Use shoe trees made of cedar to keep the shape and absorb moisture. Leather loafers tolerate light drizzle, but heavy rain can mark them and soak the sole.

title: Shoe Care Guide
heading: Waterproof boots
text: Waterproof boots are the best choice for rain, snow, and slush. Rinse off mud and road salt after wearing them, since salt dries out leather and leaves white marks. Let them dry at room temperature with the insoles removed. Reapply a waterproofing wax or spray when water stops beading on the surface.

title: Shoe Care Guide
heading: Canvas sneakers and running shoes
text: Canvas sneakers and mesh running shoes soak through quickly and are not suitable for rain. Clean canvas sneakers by hand with a soft brush and mild soap; machine washing can damage the glue. Remove the laces and insoles before cleaning and air dry them stuffed with paper.

title: Shoe Care Guide
heading: Rotating shoes
text: Avoid wearing the same pair two days in a row. Leather and the inside lining need about 24 hours to dry out fully from foot moisture, and rotating pairs makes shoes last noticeably longer.
